ruled_out.why: No series exists in either window, so no comparison is possible from this metric family; the service is neither confirmed nor excluded by it.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The user service can be cleared or implicated by comparing its error ratio in the incident window against the 16:38–17:08 baseline.

ruled_out.why: The tool explicitly distinguishes unavailable from zero — the span metrics are never emitted for this service, so absence carries no traffic or error information.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The empty result means the user service received no requests or produced no errors during the incident.

ruled_out.why: The gap spans the pre-incident baseline window equally, so it predates the incident and reflects a standing instrumentation limitation, not a change in service state.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The missing metrics are a symptom of the incident, e.g. the user service crashed or stopped reporting when the window opened.

ruled_out.why: The same absence appears for user with a stated cause of services not emitting trace-derived metrics, pointing to a general instrumentation coverage gap rather than a per-service collection fault.
ruled_out.hypothesis: The empty frontend metric family indicated a scrape or collector failure specific to frontend.

verdict.reasoning: Frontend's own code is cleared: no panic or fatal entry, and the process reached its serving state [tr_141f2b9c494c]. No deploy, flag flip, config edit, restart or human action touched frontend or consul beyond initial creation [tr_57fd4b831076][tr_c4d033b6d797], removing bad_deploy, feature_flag and a regressing config edit. A wrong Consul address is excluded because the same address stopped refusing without any re-read [tr_b46c4a6267a3]. What remains - a quiet, running frontend alerting six minutes after discovery recovered - cannot be resolved because metrics, traces and the onset-minute logs are all missing [tr_9e57cb00ad61][tr_e4ec257e6a74][tr_3c200821e5c6]. Naming a class here would be asserting past the evidence.
verdict.root_cause: The board does not establish a cause for the 17:38:25 onset. The only concrete anomaly is a ~4-second burst of Consul discovery refusals on consul:8500 right after frontend's cold start at 17:31:56 [tr_141f2b9c494c][tr_b46c4a6267a3], a bootstrap race between the frontend and consul workloads both first created at 17:31:55 by platform-automation [tr_57fd4b831076][tr_c4d033b6d797]. That burst ended at 17:32:00 and never recurred, leaving ~6.5 clean minutes before the alert [tr_b46c4a6267a3], so it is not the onset mechanism. Everything that could name the real mechanism was structurally unavailable: no span metrics for frontend or user in either window [tr_9e57cb00ad61][tr_3c200821e5c6], zero frontend traces for the hour [tr_e4ec257e6a74], and a truncated log slice covering only 17:31:56-17:32:00 [tr_141f2b9c494c]. The fault most likely lies on one of the five unmeasured edges below frontend, unidentified.

alternatives.why_not: The 8500-filtered query covered the full window without truncation and shows no refusals after 17:32:00 [tr_b46c4a6267a3]; no Consul-side log or metric was ever gathered to support ongoing degradation.
alternatives.root_cause: Consul remained unhealthy or degraded after its 17:31:55 stand-up, so frontend's later re-resolutions stalled and callers waited.

alternatives.why_not: Zero traces and no span metrics exist to attribute latency to any downstream service [tr_e4ec257e6a74][tr_3c200821e5c6]; this is a plausible shape with no evidence naming a culprit.
alternatives.root_cause: A downstream hotel-reservation service became slow after 17:32, and frontend's requests failed on waiting for it.

open_questions: What did frontend log between 17:32:00 and 17:38:30? The unfiltered query was truncated and never covered the onset minute.
Which of the five unmeasured downstream edges (user, recommendation, profile, search, reservation) was slow or erroring at onset? No per-service logs or latency data were gathered for any of them.
Is Consul itself healthy after 17:32:00? Its own logs and health were never queried - only its change history.

draft.title: Critical frontend alert with no attributable mechanism: six services affected, five unmeasured edges

sections.body:
The page came from frontend and nothing else. Severity was critical and the declared blast radius covered six services, but the only signal in hand at T+0 was that one alert. There was no accompanying dashboard movement to anchor against, because — as we discovered later — the dashboards for this service were structurally empty rather than flat.

The practical starting position: an alert onset at T+0, a service with five downstream edges (user, recommendation, profile, search, reservation), and no measurement on any of those five edges. Everything that follows is an attempt to cross one of them.
sections.heading: What the responder saw first

sections.body:
Roughly T-6m30s: the platform automation actor created the frontend service object and its first workload container. At the same second it created the consul service object and its first workload container. Both are first-creation records, not edits to anything already running.

T-6m29s: the frontend process cold-started — config read, tracing init, discovery agent init, gRPC client init, HTTP listener bound. The restart is visible in its own logs, so the process was not running continuously through the window.

T-6m29s to T-6m25s: a burst of discovery refusals. The frontend's load-balancer client could not pull instances from the discovery agent; the HTTP GET to the health endpoint came back as a refused TCP connection on port 8500 against the cluster VIP. All five downstream lookups failed identically inside that burst.

T-6m25s: last refusal line. The process finished startup and began serving about a second after boot. No further port-8500 line appears anywhere through the end of the window.

T+0: the alert. Nothing in any log, metric, or trace source we queried marks this moment.
sections.heading: Timeline as reconstructed

sections.body:
This is the one concrete anomaly on the board and it is very easy to mistake for the cause. The reasoning that led us to it: frontend logs showed exactly one class of error, and it affected every backend uniformly, which argued the problem sat at the discovery dependency rather than at any single downstream service. The change record then showed the frontend and discovery workloads were stood up in the same second by the same automation — a textbook bootstrap race where the client comes up before the registry is accepting connections.

It does not hold. A narrowed query on the port-8500 string covered the full half-hour window without truncation and showed the refusals confined to a roughly four-second burst, last line at T-6m25s, with nothing in the twenty-three minutes before the restart and nothing in the six and a half minutes between the burst and the alert. Discovery was clean for the entire approach to onset. A transient that stopped six minutes before the symptom and never recurred is not the onset mechanism.

Secondary lines also closed here: the discovery hostname resolved fine (the error text carries the VIP, so this is a refused connection and not a lookup failure); TLS was disabled at startup with no handshake errors; there was no panic, stack trace, or fatal line; and the process reached its serving state rather than crash-looping.
sections.heading: The discovery burst, and why it is not the answer

sections.body:
The change history was queried for both frontend and the discovery service across a full 24-hour window. For frontend: exactly two entries, both at T-6m30s, both automation-attributed, both creations. That closes a deploy or release, a runtime toggle, a config edit, a manual operator action, and any restart or re-roll during the window — none of those events exist in the record.

For the discovery service: same shape. Two entries at the same second, a service-level config creation and a first-ever workload creation, again automation-attributed. There was no prior running instance for a config edit to regress, no restart loop, no reschedule or eviction, and no earlier change in the window that could have drifted into failure.

One caveat worth carrying forward: the frontend query returned only service-scoped entries. Changes to frontend's dependencies are unassessed, not confirmed absent.
sections.heading: Dead end: the change log

sections.body:
The error-ratio query against Prometheus for frontend did not return an empty series — it failed outright, with an explicit note that this backend holds no span-derived metrics for the service because the service sends no traces that become metrics. The baseline window thirty minutes earlier is equally unpopulated, so there is no before/after comparison available from this source.

The same query against the user service failed the same way for the same stated reason. That is the useful part of running it twice: the gap is not a per-service collection failure and not a scrape outage, and widening the range or retrying will not change the result. It is a standing coverage limitation that predates the incident.

The trap here, and it is a real one at 3am: reading an empty panel as a healthy service. Nothing about frontend's or user's health — traffic, errors, latency, saturation — can be inferred from these results in either direction.
sections.heading: Dead end: metrics were never going to answer this

sections.body:
A trace query for frontend over a full hour spanning the incident returned nothing at all. Not a filtered subset coming back empty — no spans for the service, period. That means no outbound call spans, no dependency edges, and no span statuses to read.

The consequence is blunt: tracing neither implicates nor exonerates any downstream service. All five edges remain equally open on this evidence. And the totality of the absence is itself a signal — a degraded-but-serving frontend would normally still emit error or long-duration spans, so emission or ingestion for this service should be treated as a live question in its own right rather than assumed healthy.
sections.heading: Dead end: tracing

sections.body:
No cause is established for the T+0 onset. The only concrete anomaly on the board is the discovery burst, and it is temporally disqualified by six and a half clean minutes. Everything that could have named the real mechanism was unavailable by construction: no span metrics for frontend or user in either window, zero frontend traces for the hour, and a log slice that was truncated down to four seconds of cold-start output.

The failure most plausibly sits on one of the five unmeasured edges below frontend, but we cannot say which, and we have no evidence that would distinguish between them. Confidence is low. No fix class is proposed; proposing one here would be guessing.
sections.heading: Where this landed

sections.body:
First: what did frontend log between T-6m25s and T+5s? The unfiltered log query was truncated to the cold-start cluster and never reached the onset minute. Re-run it windowed tightly on the minute around T+0, or paginate past the truncation. This is the highest-value gap on the board.

Second: which of the five downstream edges was slow or erroring at onset? No per-service logs and no latency data were gathered for any of user, recommendation, profile, search, or reservation. Pull logs for each directly; do not route through frontend's view of them.

Third: is the discovery service itself healthy after T-6m25s? We queried only its change history, never its own logs or health endpoint. The burst stopping on its own is consistent with it coming up correctly, but that was inferred from the client side, not confirmed from the server side.

Fourth, lower priority but worth a ticket: frontend emits no traces and no span-derived metrics. That is why this record ends where it does.
sections.heading: Open questions for whoever picks this up

proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is that the incident continues unmitigated while the alert is live, and the time spent on further investigation is time the alerted frontend stays degraded. If the true mechanism is a frontend process-state fault that a restart would clear, this abstention leaves it running. Against that: acting on a low-confidence 'unknown' verdict risks a restart that recreates the known 17:31:56 bootstrap race, producing a fresh all-backend discovery gap and destroying the in-process state and the very log continuity needed to find the real cause — converting an unexplained degradation into a second, self-inflicted one with the original still undiagnosed.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if a subsequent untruncated log slice over 17:32:00–17:38:30 shows a mechanism that one of rollback_image, revert_config or restart_service addresses — for example renewed consul:8500 refusals continuing through onset (would point at consul process state), a frontend OOM/goroutine-leak or connection-pool-exhaustion signature (would point at restart_service on frontend), or a downstream service logging errors from a recorded image or config change inside the window (would point at rollback or revert on that service). It is also wrong if a stakeholder judges that a blind frontend restart is cheap enough to try despite an unknown mechanism; I do not, because the only measured consequence of a frontend cold start in this incident is a 4-second total discovery outage across all five backends [tr_b46c4a6267a3]. Note separately that no action taken here could be confirmed by metrics: frontend and user have no span-derived series in either the incident or baseline window [tr_9e57cb00ad61][tr_3c200821e5c6] and frontend emitted zero traces for the hour [tr_e4ec257e6a74], so the only available confirmation channel is Loki logs. An unobservable fix is a second reason to hold.
proposal.blast_radius: No service is touched, so no caller sees a change. For contrast, the action not taken: a frontend restart would be seen by every external client of frontend and would momentarily break its outbound edges to user, recommendation, profile, search and reservation during re-resolution; a restart or rollback of any one of those five would be seen by frontend as reset connections on that edge. The investigative follow-ups proposed instead (log and metric queries) are read-only and visible to nobody.
proposal.expected_effect: No action proposed, so no effect is expected. Nothing about the system should change as a result of this proposal. Concretely: none of the three buildable actions has its preconditions met. rollback_image requires a prior image tag and a deploy/image change inside the window — frontend's change log holds only a service-object creation and a first container creation at 17:31:55, with no predecessor image recorded [tr_57fd4b831076], and the same is true for the only other service with change data, consul [tr_c4d033b6d797]. revert_config requires a prior configuration and a config change inside the window — again only a creation record exists, and the one configured address under suspicion (consul:8500) was demonstrated to become reachable without any change [tr_b46c4a6267a3]. restart_service requires evidence pointing at process state: the only process-state signal is a cold start at 17:31:56 whose discovery-refusal burst ended at 17:32:00 and never recurred, leaving ~6.5 clean minutes before the 17:38:25 onset [tr_b46c4a6267a3] — restarting frontend would re-run exactly the bootstrap race that was already ruled out as the onset mechanism. The correct next step is investigative, not remedial: an untruncated frontend log query covering 17:32:00–17:38:30, and per-service logs for the five unmeasured downstream edges.
